newsitem.title: USA: Plan for more US equity option strikes hits snags.
newsitem.headline: Plan for more US equity option strikes hits snags.

text.p: Two of the five U.S. equity options exchanges hope to expand the list of individual equity options with 2-1/2 point strike prices, but the plan is running into resistance from regulators and some market participants.
"It would be horrendous," said Harrison Roth at Cowen & Co, contending that it would add too many new options.

In July, the Philadelphia Stock Exchange (PHLX) and the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) separately asked the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) for permission to double their list of stocks with 2-1/2-point strike prices.
Market participants who attended an industry group meeting earlier this week said the proposals were on a back burner.
"The SEC more or less put a squash on it," said one industry source. "So it doesn't look like there will be any expansion for some time now."
The SEC approved a pilot plan in 1995 for the five options exchanges to introduce 2-1/2-point strike prices on options on 100 stocks priced between $25 and $50.

The exchanges then divided up the 100 securities, with the Chicago Board Options Exchange (CBOE) getting 28, the American Stock Exchange (AMEX) 22, the PHLX 18, the Pacific Stock Exchange 18 and the NYSE 14.
The SEC extended the plan for another year in July.
Despite the apparent snag in expanding the program, the other options exchanges said they favor the 2-1/2-point strikes.
"We would be happy to have the program increased to give us more flexibility," a CBOE spokesman said.
The Pacific Stock Exchange plans to file a proposal to expand its allocation, a spokesman said.
A spokesman at the American Stock Exchange said the exchange had not yet decided on a plan of action.
Michael Schwartz at Oppenheimer & Co said the greater number of strikes has increased liquidity in those issues, which include Quaker Oats Co and Pepsico Inc.
But with new options and industry indexes constantly being listed, some options participants said adding more strike prices would overwhelm an already crowded market.
"If they're serious about it, the other (options) exchanges are going to file for it also and we're going to have a ridiculous number of strikes," Roth said.
"It's already ridiculous, so what's a little more?" said Jay Shartsis, head of options trading at R.F. Lafferty & Co.
Schwartz, who heads the Committee on Options (COOP), an industry group, said an overriding concern is to not have 2-1/2-point strike prices on all options.
In its SEC filing, the PHLX said the benefits of expanding the list would include the ability to more closely tailor strategies to precise movements of the underlying securities.
Not all options participants oppose the plan.
"I think they're good in that you have more strike prices near the money," said Marty Kearney at PTI Securities.
